item.description: arXiv:2609.08572v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems (MAS) achieve strong performance by employing specialized multiple agents, yet their performance depends on the prompt design of each agent. For MAS prompt optimization, textual gradient methods that guide prompt updates using natural-language feedback have emerged as a leading paradigm. In this paper, we identify limitations in two stages of existing textual gradient approaches: gradient extraction and gradient aggregation. In gradient extraction, previous works select a prompt to update without verifying whether modifying it resolves the failure, and derive gradients without agent-level supervision over the corresponding agent's intermediate output. In gradient aggregation, individual gradients are randomly grouped and concatenated, often mixing unrelated failure modes and producing prompts that fail to generalize. To address these limitations, we propose AgentGrad, a prompt optimization framework for multi-agent systems based on sequential intervention and semantic textual gradient abstraction. For each failure, sequential intervention injects a hint into one agent at a time to identify the target agent whose modification resolves the failure. The modified output of the target agent then serves as agent-level supervision for extracting a fine-grained gradient. Semantic textual gradient abstraction clusters semantically similar gradients to prevent mixing unrelated failure modes, and abstracts each cluster into a generalized gradient that captures the shared corrective pattern. Experimental results show that AgentGrad achieves state-of-the-art performance across five MAS benchmarks while reducing wall-clock optimization time by 2.5 times and optimization cost by 21.8% on average compared to the next-best baselines. Our code is available at https://github.com/mlvlab/AgentGrad.

item.title: LLMs as Post-hoc Auditors of Physiological Plausibility in Symbolic Regression: A Clinician-Evaluated Case Study
item.description: arXiv:2609.11431v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Genetic programming and its variants, such as grammatical evolution, are widely used in symbolic regression to derive mathematical expressions from multivariate data. In addition to predictive accuracy, models are appreciated for their potential to provide interpretability, offering explicit equations that relate input variables to outcomes. However, achieving interpretability and plausibility remains challenging, as evolved models may be complex or scientifically inconsistent. In this study, we explore whether large language models (LLMs) can assist in improving the interpretability of symbolic regression models generated by evolutionary computation methods. Building on our previous work on estimating body fat percentage using grammar-based genetic programming, we investigate LLMs as post-processing tools to analyze and rank evolved expressions by interpretability and physiological plausibility. Four symbolic expressions are analyzed by three LLMs over three repeated runs, and the resulting interpretations and rankings are assessed by a panel of three clinicians. Across the three LLMs, comparative model-ranking outputs received more favorable clinician assessments than isolated term-level interpretations. However, the LLMs also produced physiologically and mathematically questionable explanations, indicating that they are better suited to comparative auditing under expert oversight than to autonomous validation.

item.title: MoMHa: Multi-Objective Optimization of LLM Harnesses over Accuracy, Safety, and Tokens
item.description: arXiv:2609.30967v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Most work on improving large language models treats accuracy as the sole objective. We argue that the harness, the Python code surrounding the model that constructs prompts, routes calls, and parses outputs, is a first-class design surface whose quality is inherently multi-objective: an accurate harness that refuses no unsafe request, or that consumes an order of magnitude more tokens, is not a good harness. We present Meta-Harness, a system that casts harness design as search over three per-domain objectives (accuracy, behavioural safety, and token cost) solved by an agentic proposer (Claude Code) with full filesystem access to prior harness source, execution traces, and scoring artifacts. Our central finding is that a singlephase joint-reward proposer (MoMHa) outperforms every alternative, including a two-phase "accuracy then tokens" ablation, scalar-only feedback, and an accuracy-only baseline. We evaluate on seventeen domains: seven synthetic capability suites, seven real-world public benchmarks (HumanEval, MBPP, Spider, FEVER, MMLU-Pro, LawBench, NuminaMath), and three U-SafeBench-derived user-specific safety domains, using a 12-model fleet spanning four families. On the synthetic track MoMHa achieves a joint mean of 0.482 versus 0.198-0.422 for ten baselines, winning $7 / 10$ per-domain columns; on the real-world track it scores 0.461 versus 0.377 for the strongest baseline (DSPy), winning 5/7 columns, demonstrating that harness strategies transfer to unseen benchmarks without retraining on 8 of 12 target models. MoMHa attains the highest measured behavioral safety composite (U-SafeBench, 0.781) and uses 95 fewer tokens per example than the two-phase alternative. We will release all harness code, evaluation infrastructure, and crossmodel logs.

item.title: Programs-of-Layers in LLMs through the Lens of Cortical Areas
item.description: arXiv:2609.31360v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Inference in LLMs is conventionally a fixed-depth, fixed-order forward pass through every layer, regardless of how difficult the input is. The human brain does not work this way. Using the thalamus as a central hub, it routes information flexibly to all regions of the cortex according to demand. Li et al. (2026) recently showed, with program-of-layers (PoLar), that transformers can be given an analogous flexibility if their layers are treated as a library of functions rather than a fixed sequence. Performance improves over the standard forward pass when each input is dynamically routed through an adaptive sequence of skipped or repeated contiguous layer blocks. Reconstructing PoLar's diagnostic Monte Carlo Tree Search in more detail across 6 models, we reproduce several of its findings: skipping outperforms the standard pass, repeating outperforms skipping, and combining both outperforms either alone. Shorter programs suffice for easier questions, while harder questions require more layer repeats. For their main claim, the learned router's gain, we find what drives it. Under their setup, the router gains by repairing the format of the model's answers, which a single fixed program, selected on validation questions, does better. In our setup, with a prompt that already fixes the format, a larger data split and our search, its top prediction collapses to the standard pass on every model, although its top-5 programs together still gain. Beyond reproduction, we find in our setup that a small fixed menu of programs solves far more questions than the standard pass, and that programs which correct errors are brittle: undoing a single edit typically breaks the correction. PoLar mirrors principles of thalamo-cortical coordination between cortical-area-like transformer layers, although a working thalamus analogue, a router that picks a better program per input, remains to be found.

item.title: Structured Sparse Memory for Recurrent Reasoning
item.description: arXiv:2609.33270v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Recurrent models trained from scratch have recently become competitive on ARC-style reasoning tasks, but the usual framing around small recurrent backbones overlooks two important parts of the system: task-conditioned memory and synthetic augmentation data. We study this regime through CHARM, a compact hybrid ARC model that combines recurrent reasoning with structured task memory, synthetic data, and inference-time aggregation. In existing approaches, task-conditioned memory supplies a large hidden source of capacity, reaching more than 30x the size of the recurrent backbone. We introduce a compositional sparse embedding (CoSE) for task conditioning that reduces learned task-memory parameters by over 90% while improving pass@2 in controlled ARC ablations. We also introduce Re-ARC2, a set of programs that generate and verify new examples for all ARC-AGI-2 training tasks. Combining these ingredients, our system reaches 84% pass@2 on ARC-AGI-1 and 46.7% pass@2 on ARC-AGI-2 public evaluation. Structured memory also enables adaptation with only 512 parameters per unseen puzzle, and its benefits generalize to other domains. Our code, dataset, and model checkpoints are available at https://github.com/water-vapor/charm.

item.title: Code Owns the Simulation, Jev Owns the Evaluation
item.description: arXiv:2610.01834v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Judgment models such as \jev{} return, in a single call and without reasoning text, a probability for each described option. This makes them attractive as an agent's action-selection layer, but it is unclear which decisions they can be trusted with. We test \jev{} on reflection tests, one-shot matrix games, the text game ALFWorld and robot control, and find a sharp boundary. \jev{} succeeds when the right option can be judged from what the input describes, which we call \emph{evaluation}. Specifically, it solves 99\% of the counterintuitive Cognitive Reflection Test questions. However, it fails when the right option depends on \emph{simulation} (i.e., predicting something not in the input), such as the opponent's action or the subgoal that must come first. In games, \jev{} plays suboptimally as if its rational opponent acted at random, because the opponent's action is not given. In ALFWorld, \jev{} favors commands that mention an object or place named in the task description. For example, given the task ``put a clean knife in the drawer'', \jev{} carries an unwashed knife straight to the drawer instead of first washing it at the sink. Surprisingly, many of these failures are not due to a lack of knowledge. Asked separately what the opponent will do, \jev{} usually answers correctly, and it responds well given the opponent's action. It fails when one call must both perform the simulation and evaluate based on it. This suggests letting code make the prediction or simulation. When code supplies it, such as a lookahead in ALFWorld and physics simulation in robot control, \jev{} becomes an expert controller through its general evaluation ability.

item.title: Continual Graph Memory and Community Infrastructure for AI-Assisted Mathematical Discovery
item.description: arXiv:2610.02945v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Mathematical discovery requires preserving partial ideas and the evidence supporting their reuse. We present Ansatz, a research harness whose continual graph memory separates model-accepted claims and dependencies from curated exploration, and Ansatze, a community platform for inspecting, guiding and checking this work. On First Proof, Ansatz recorded nine local verifier closures in each of two ten-problem batches; a partial result in the Second Batch also counted as a pass under the study's criterion. These model-assessed outcomes include continued searches and differ from expert validation. Component studies and re-review expose disagreements and their dependency reach. Open-problem investigations produced candidate results, with five Lean formalizations reported. The platform connects problem discovery, research records, manuscript analysis and formal checking while preserving distinct evidence states. Together, these systems support cumulative human-AI research through persistent investigation and inspectable contributions.

item.title: HarnessNet: Feedback-driven Hierarchical Joint Harness Evolution for Multi-agent Systems
item.description: arXiv:2610.15221v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: AI agents can evolve by using environment feedback to revise their harnesses, the software managing model inputs, tool use, memory, and execution, while keeping foundation models frozen. Existing studies focus on single agents, leaving joint harness evolution in multi-agent systems (MAS) underexplored. A single global optimizer faces growing context and workload as the system scales, while access restrictions may prevent sharing agent internals or system-wide feedback. We propose HarnessNet, a framework for hierarchical harness evolution in MAS. Its basic unit, Agentron, comprises an evolvable forward harness, a foundation model, and a local optimizer that can observe and modify only that harness. Agentrons form a layered graph through which environment feedback propagates backward, with upstream optimizers receiving node-specific feedback from the downstream layer. This decomposes joint harness evolution into smaller, coordinated tasks with separate contexts, reducing individual optimizers' context and workload while keeping access local. Optimizers need not access all agent trajectories or raw environment feedback. Experiments on AgentBench with multiple foundation models demonstrate the feasibility of training HarnessNet. Compared with a single global optimizer, HarnessNet achieves comparable performance gains while respecting local privacy and requiring fewer tokens and less time per optimizer call. A migration study shows that the evolved harnesses remain jointly effective after replacing the foundation models, suggesting transferability across models.

item.title: AuthGateBench: Benchmarking LLMs as Authorization Gate
item.description: arXiv:2610.16426v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Automated approval systems let coding agents execute high-risk actions with minimal human oversight by delegating the authorization decision to a classifier, typically a large language model (LLM). Such systems, adopted in tools like Claude Code and Codex, remain vulnerable to failure modes such as scope escalation, where the agent takes actions exceeding what the user authorized. Existing benchmarks focus mainly on malicious requests, evaluating refusal under an implicit policy. We introduce AuthGateBench, the first policy-guided benchmark for authorization gating under benign requests. We implement a novel pipeline where an LLM generates contrast pairs with identical action and trajectory but differing request, flipping the label between block and allow. This allows us to assess whether models reason over context rather than the action alone. We further examine whether auxiliary environment signals can help models make better decisions. The resulting benchmark comprises 1,400 instances spanning five failure modes drawn from real-world Claude Code incidents. Evaluations show accuracy degrades unevenly across failure modes as models over-rely on internal safety alignment, and models still block most actions even when explicitly authorized, revealing unstable rather than deterministic decisions; retrospectively retrieved environment signals, however, substantially improve authorization accuracy.

item.title: SteadyThought: Mitigating LLM Under-Thinking via Thought-Level Preference Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2610.25045v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Flexible switching between reasoning trajectories (i.e., thought switching) has significantly enhanced the reasoning capabilities of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs). However, existing models often switch excessively yet fail to sustain promising reasoning thoughts, a phenomenon termed "under-thinking". While recent efforts suppress switching to mitigate this, such over-correction may discard valuable trajectories. To address this challenge, we propose Steady Thought (ST), a novel thought-level preference optimization framework. ST formalizes under-thinking as a preference issue at switching points, forcing single-path continuations from identified points to yield high-quality reasoning. Then, ST performs thought-level preference optimization by treating the newly generated response as preferred and the original one as dis-preferred. Experiments across multiple models and datasets show that ST effectively reduces token consumption, achieving reductions of up to 63.8%, while maintaining strong reasoning accuracy. Further analysis suggests that ST helps models acquire a generalizable ability to reduce redundant switching across domains and languages. Code is available at https://github.com/MIRALab-USTC/SteadyThought.

item.title: CoRS: Fast Neural Flexible Job-Shop Scheduling via Composite Interval State Reuse
item.description: arXiv:2610.26239v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Neural solvers for the Flexible Job-Shop Scheduling Problem (FJSP) typically refresh graph representations and update feasibility after every operation--machine decision. However, only feasibility must remain exact at every step, whereas graph encoding is substantially more expensive and can potentially be refreshed less frequently. We present CoRS, which decouples them: an interval-level graph representation is reused across multiple sequential decisions, while a stepwise feasibility state is updated after every action. This two-timescale design amortizes graph encoding without parallelizing action generation or relaxing scheduling constraints. CoRS further develops a feasibility-preserving composite-interval decoding scheme with dynamic constraint tracking and boundary state synchronization, which reduces representation refresh frequency while maintaining continuous feasible schedule construction. Furthermore, to alleviate representation staleness caused by interval-level state reuse, CoRS introduces enhanced static features as a compensation mechanism. By providing more comprehensive structural information of the scheduling problem, these features improve the model's perception of overall problem characteristics. Extensive experiments on synthetic and multiple public FJSP benchmarks demonstrate that CoRS significantly reduces inference time while maintaining competitive solution quality, achieving favorable speed-quality trade-offs under tight wall-clock budgets and low-latency scenarios.

item.title: REFLEX: RNA Ensemble Generation via Flexibility-Calibrated Stochastic Bridge
item.description: arXiv:2610.26261v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: RNA molecules often function through multiple experimentally observed conformational states. A central challenge is to capture ensemble diversity without sacrificing structural fidelity: samples may collapse toward averaged representative structures or drift into unsupported conformational regions. We introduce REFLEX (RNA Ensemble generation calibrated by FLEXibility), a sequence-conditioned generator for RNA backbone-frame ensembles based on a heteroscedastic stochastic bridge on SE(3). During training, experimental B-factors calibrate residue-wise bridge widths, exposing each observed conformer through local perturbation neighborhoods with residue-specific scales while keeping constrained regions sharper. A learned flexibility condition guides the bridge-field network to recover target conformer-specific frames from these calibrated noisy states. At inference, REFLEX uses only the input sequence, requiring no MSA-subsampling heuristics. On a multi-conformer RNA benchmark, REFLEX achieves the best precision-recall trade-off for ensemble coverage across evaluation thresholds, while recovery-stress ablations indicate gains in target-frame recovery under stronger perturbations.

item.title: HarnessMM: Recursive Self-Improvement for Harness Token Efficiency
item.description: arXiv:2610.32813v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: HarnessMinusMinus (HarnessMM) is a research project on improving the efficiency of agent harnesses, the software coordinating model reasoning, tool execution, and feedback. This technical report consolidates its shared framework, implementations, and empirical studies across coding, tool-based, and visual-agent settings. Agent harnesses often invoke reasoning after each tool result, even when earlier calls have already determined subsequent actions. HarnessMM addresses this overhead through guarded decision reuse and recursive self-improvement (RSI). RSI refines author prompts, context settings, and adapter rules using training feedback, with validation selecting deployment configurations. At inference time, a controller reuses resolved decisions while keeping actor weights fixed. Executable Decision Graphs encode actions, arguments, dependencies, and guards. Guarded Decision Reuse activates eligible decisions from observed feedback, while Certified Callback Substitution executes them through native tool interfaces, replacing redundant reasoning callbacks. The original actor resumes when new reasoning is required or reuse conditions are unmet. On HumanEval, HarnessMM preserves Codex success at 90.82\% while reducing tokens per task from 66.72k to 47.02k (29.54\% saving). For DeepSeek Harness, success improves from 71.43\% to 85.71\% while tokens decrease from 96.28k to 11.62k (87.93\% saving). An MBPP ablation shows 26.91\% lower cost than single-use graphs and 19.52\% lower cost than retained callbacks. The report also summarizes the HarnessMM-V visual-agent study and documents optimization overhead and execution time where measured. Together, these studies investigate guarded decision reuse across diverse agent harness settings. Code is available at https://github.com/YuhuaJiang2002/HarnessMM.

item.title: DecoyCount: Evaluating Visual-Reasoning Misalignment in Counting
item.description: arXiv:2610.34855v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Visual counting benchmarks report whether vision-language models produce the correct number, but not whether errors arise from perception or reasoning. We introduce DecoyCount, a benchmark built from 1,586 real-world images with designed decoys across seven mechanisms, along with paired prompts: a neutral question, a matched alignment cue, and a novel multi-hop, multi-image question that situates the same counting problem in a realistic scenario. Using this design, we find that counting failures are induced partly by visual misalignment: models can execute the intended counting process when cue-guided but fail to select it unaided, and we term this difference in accuracy the reasoning-alignment gap. Despite being highly capable on general reasoning, frontier models remain below 50% accuracy on our benchmark, while alignment gaps range from 12.1-22.1 percentage points; strikingly, we observe that more capable models, greater thinking budgets, and agentic processes often induce larger gaps. Because humans may bring context that models lack, we test whether textual underspecification contributes to misalignment using a scenario-based multi-hop condition without explicit hinting, but this added context does not improve aggregate performance. Our analysis concludes that stronger general reasoning does not by itself generalize to aligned visual reasoning, leaving misalignment with human visual expectations as a substantial component of the remaining deficit. DecoyCount and the evaluation code are released at https://github.com/elorian-ai/decoycount.

item.title: Radial Kernel Attention for Global Feature Exchange in Polymer Machine Learning Force Fields
item.description: arXiv:2610.41675v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We introduce Radial Kernel Attention (RKA) for long-range modeling in polymer machine learning force fields. Existing approaches often rely on local neighbor graphs, which limit communication across polymer chains and their surrounding environments, whereas explicit all-pair attention incurs quadratic computational cost. RKA maps interatomic distances from the cluster centroid to learned radial features and combines their kernelized overlap with content-dependent queries and keys. Factorized aggregation and readout enable global feature exchange at linear complexity in the number of atoms for fixed feature dimensions. To ensure physically consistent predictions, we insert the invariant scalar update between EquiformerV3 local blocks and obtain conservative forces by differentiating the total energy, including its dependence on radial coordinate . Our models are trained on official OPoly26 training set for 12 epochs and evaluated directly after training on the complete official validation set. A matched 5M comparison shows that RKA reduces per-atom energy and force MAEs by 67.4% and 36.3%, respectively. The 20M RKA model attains a total-energy MAE of 15.81 meV (per-atom MAE of 0.1182 meV/atom) and a force MAE of 2.619 meV/Angstrom,improving all three metrics over UMA-S-1.2 and UMA-S-1.2.1 on the same validation structures. RKA provides a compact pathway for information exchange beyond local graph connectivity in polymer machine learning force fields.

item.title: Seeing What Matters, Verifying What Pays: Load-Adaptive Speculative Decoding for Vision-Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.01617v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates vision-language model (VLM) inference without altering the output distribution, yet two factors limit its gains. Existing drafters either lack the image evidence required for visually grounded tokens or pay to condition on every visual token, although a short draft block typically depends on only a few image regions. Moreover, the value of verifying additional candidates varies with GPU load, so no fixed verification structure is efficient across serving conditions. We present Uni-LaSpec, a block-parallel speculative decoding framework that addresses both factors. To improve draft quality, Uni-LaSpec reuses the verifier's own attention: the query retained from the preceding verification ranks the cached, int8-quantized visual keys, and a cross-layer vote selects a few visual tokens that the drafter fuses through gated cross-attention. Acceptance-aware training further weights each draft position by its contribution to the accepted prefix. To allocate verification, a marginal-cost criterion selects the structure per request and per round: draft trees exploit idle verifier capacity under light load, whereas a dynamic head truncates linear drafts under heavy load. Across six VLMs from three model families and 17 text and multimodal benchmarks, selecting eight visual tokens retains at least 98.6% of the acceptance obtained from the full image at sub-millisecond selection cost. With greedy decoding at concurrency one, Uni-LaSpec achieves up to 5.11x text and 3.24x multimodal throughput over autoregressive decoding. Across six load levels and three GPU types, it outperforms autoregressive decoding in every setting and matches or exceeds the best fixed verification strategy in 123 of 144 settings; under bursty arrivals, it reduces mean end-to-end latency by 47.6% relative to linear verification.

item.title: LUCA: A Synthetic World for Experimental Reasoning
item.description: arXiv:2611.03100v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: An experimental agent can succeed for the wrong reasons. Evaluations, however, often focus on the outcome, not the experiments, evidence, and inferences that produced it. We introduce LUCA, a configurable synthetic world for evaluating this process under fully known ground truth. Agents learn unknown regulatory systems through budgeted experimentation, then predict unseen interventions, diagnose hidden faults, and attempt rescues. This setup allows us to evaluate experiment selection, prediction, diagnosis, and intervention separately. Across seven frontier LLMs and three baselines, these capabilities dissociate sharply. Agents frequently rescue malfunctioning systems while diagnosing the wrong fault; diagnosis varies 7x across models while prediction varies only 1.4x. Models also adopt surprisingly different experimental strategies, and greater exploration does not reliably yield better performance. In one failure mode, agents often perform the experiment needed to distinguish competing causes, but still fail to use the resulting evidence. LUCA turns these hidden failures into measurable behaviours, providing a controlled environment to study where experimental agents succeed and fail. Code: https://github.com/RelationRx/luca.

item.title: AceAction-5M: Hierarchical Goals for Generalist Action Learning Across 3D Game Worlds
item.description: arXiv:2611.04241v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Video games provide a practical setting for collecting vision-language-action (VLA) data, whose acquisition in physical environments is costly. Existing datasets, however, remain limited by restricted game coverage, sparse language supervision, or temporal hierarchies that do not necessarily reflect changes in task objectives. We introduce AceAction, a dataset of human gameplay across multiple 3D games for learning skill composition and subgoal transitions. AceAction organizes demonstrations around complete tasks, linking overall instructions, ordered subgoals, and local skill instructions to temporally aligned visual observations and keyboard-and-mouse actions. To construct these annotations, we develop a vision-language model pipeline that identifies subgoals from changes in objectives or interaction targets, anchors navigation goals to visually recognizable waypoints, and composes adjacent subgoals into task instructions. The resulting demonstrations cover navigation, reconnaissance, combat, interaction, and recovery, with explicit stage boundaries that connect task progression to fine-grained control. We assess annotation quality through model-based verification and human inspection. An audit of 500 trajectories yields a 95.8% pass rate across independent reviewer assessments. AceAction provides a data foundation for studying how agents execute, combine, and switch skills to follow complex instructions in dynamic game environments.

item.title: Treating the Symptom, Missing the Cause: Anatomy of a Scientific Reasoning Failure
item.description: arXiv:2611.04473v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Scientific agents can find interventions that work without understanding why they do. We study this failure mode in controlled synthetic regulatory systems, where agents must experimentally identify a hidden fault and rescue the resulting phenotype. Across seven LLMs, every model restores the healthy phenotypes more often than it identifies the fault. Claude Opus 4.6 and Sonnet 4.6 rescue every organism while diagnosing only 55% and 35% of them. This failure is not simply due to insufficient exploration or unavailable evidence. In most cases, the cause is experimentally identifiable, and agents encounter evidence that distinguishes competing causes in 91% of relevant sessions, and still frequently misdiagnose the system. Targeted probes reveal where experimental reasoning breaks down. Models reliably interpret decisive evidence and revise hypotheses when the causal comparison is explicit, and can locate that evidence within a full experimental record. However, they struggle to predict the outcome of the experiment under each competing cause, a necessary step in using the observed result to distinguish between them. Agents can therefore gather the right evidence and still infer the wrong cause. As AI systems take on a growing role in synthesising scientific evidence, these findings highlight the need to evaluate how they use evidence to reach causal conclusions, alongside whether their interventions succeed.

item.title: A Definition of Catastrophic Performance
item.description: arXiv:2611.06219v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A central challenge in AI is specifying objectives that align with human preferences. While existing theoretical results elucidate how misspecification impacts performance, they typically do not distinguish between merely suboptimal and catastrophic outcomes. To enable rigorous analysis of catastrophic risk from AI misalignment, we introduce a formal definition of catastrophic performance. Our definition is based on two reference values. The first, baseline value, captures the value attained if no agent is deployed. The second, orthogonal value, captures the value of a trajectory that is unrelated to human preferences, in a sense we describe. Orthogonal value is typically far worse than baseline value. We interpret these reference values through examples in which past human activity has altered the state of the environment to human benefit. Starting at the resulting state, an AI agent is deployed with the goal of accelerating further progress. Catastrophic performance represents this agent's undoing of benefits afforded by human activity.

item.title: AdaFloor: Adaptive Floor Planning and Rank-Time Reuse for Long-Tail MoE RL Rollouts
item.description: arXiv:2611.06984v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Synchronous MoE reinforcement-learning post-training suffers from response-length imbalance. Existing methods reduce request tails, yet completed ranks remain bound to Expert Parallelism (EP) collectives and expert ownership. In a representative 16-accelerator Qwen3-30B-A3B rollout, this dummy run traps 32.83% of rank-time. AdaFloor converts this EP-coupled capacity into bounded leases for auxiliary work to improve system resource efficiency through rank-time reuse. Historical prompt-tail prediction and a calibrated guard construct the KV-safe layout. AdaFloor then selects the floor-specific safe quorum schedule with the largest predicted release area. Its runtime shrinks the EP group and leases detached ranks until full-world restoration. Across three updated-policy seeds on DeepScaleR mathematical reasoning rollouts, its capacity-oriented Natural floor2 configuration with TailGuard reduces Vanilla's 29393.9 rank-seconds of dummy run by 96.15%. Rollout shortening eliminates 18693.6 rank-seconds, while coordinated exits convert another 9568.6 rank-seconds into reusable capacity, leaving 1131.7 rank-seconds. For sidecar reuse, its Planned residency floor4 configuration without TailGuard serves 3134 Qwen3-8B GSM8K queries per epoch at 99.46% accuracy and incurs only a 2 to 3% primary throughput reduction against the same configuration with sidecar execution disabled. Its latency-oriented Planned residency floor4 configuration with TailGuard reduces rollout time by 24.09% relative to Vanilla and by 2.31% relative to LengthSort with TailGuard. On public Eurus-2-RL code rollouts with the same model and 16-rank topology, AdaFloor reduces rollout time by 20.56% and dummy run by 89.13% while generated work and mean reward remain stable.

item.title: BabyTheorist: A Benchmark for Learning to Theorize the World from Observation Alone
item.description: arXiv:2611.08177v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: How would we know whether a machine truly understands the world? We argue that one key capability is observational theory learning: acquiring reusable theories from pure observations and applying them to new situations. Current visual reasoning benchmarks focus primarily on the latter, presenting each task as a few-shot puzzle grouped by a common rule. We introduce BabyTheorist, a benchmark for controlled training and evaluation of observational theory learning. BabyTheorist generates continual streams of before-after visual observations from hidden compositional programs; during training, learners see only the resulting transitions, with no program labels, task identities, or support sets. To support theory learning and evaluation, BabyTheorist controls the program language, a curriculum over program complexity, recurring frequent subprograms, and a continual train-test protocol with level skipping. Seven representative baselines plateau well below ceiling, with the gap widening as the curriculum advances---evidence that BabyTheorist isolates a capability current program-learning approaches do not yet address.

item.title: Stay on the Manifold: Hierarchical Bayesian Trajectory-Family Transfer for Sparse-Target Reconstruction and Sampling
item.description: arXiv:2310.07801v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Where should reconstructions and new samples lie when a few observations reveal only fragments of a trajectory? We propose hierarchical Bayesian trajectory principal-manifold sampling (HB-TPM), which learns a family of smooth curves from ordered source tasks and adapts it to sparse targets. For unordered vectors, alternating progression assignments and coefficient updates estimate trajectory structure between and beyond the observed shots under the learned source family. Observation-aware extensions connect the trajectory prior to photon arrivals and image-encoded cardiac cycles. Our analysis characterizes the coefficient directions supplied by the prior and bounds sampling error conditional on curve recovery. Across 30 held-out vector tasks, HB-TPM reduces mean sliced-Wasserstein distance by 21.0-41.8% relative to a source-adapted VAE. Prior-strength and sampling ablations identify coefficient shrinkage as the main supported mechanism. On 100 simulated photon records, adaptation lowers mean relative trajectory RMSE by 50.2% versus target-only fitting and 23.6% versus source-mean prediction. Across three training seeds and five folds on 98 cardiac sequences, HB-TPM with latent-MSE training achieves the best mean reconstruction among the tested configurations. Together, the results demonstrate trajectory-family transfer for sparse-target reconstruction and trajectory-centered sampling when source and target tasks share comparable progression structure.

item.title: Differentiable Nonlinear Model Predictive Control
item.description: arXiv:2505.01353v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The efficient computation of parametric solution sensitivities is a key challenge in the integration of learning-enhanced methods with nonlinear model predictive control, as their availability is crucial for many learning algorithms. This paper discusses the computation of solution sensitivities of general nonlinear programs using the implicit function theorem and smoothed optimality conditions treated in interior-point methods (IPM). We introduce sequential barrier quadratic programming (SBQP), which generalizes SQP with an IPM quadratic programming (QP) solver by allowing the barrier parameter to approach a prescribed nonnegative target value, recovering classical SQP when this target is zero. Previous works are limited to convex or unconstrained formulations, or lack an implementation for efficient sensitivity evaluation. The publication is accompanied by an efficient open-source implementation within the `acados` framework, providing both forward and adjoint sensitivities for general optimal control problems, achieving speedups exceeding 3x over the state-of-the-art solvers `mpc.pytorch` and `cvxpygen`.

item.title: Equivariant Spherical Transformer for Efficient Molecular Modeling
item.description: arXiv:2505.23086v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Equivariant Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have significantly advanced the modeling of 3D molecular structure by leveraging group representations. However, message passing built only from exactly equivariant operations can have restricted practical expressiveness at a fixed representation degree. We introduce the Equivariant Spherical Transformer (EST), a plug-and-play module that applies Transformer attention to spherical spatial representations obtained from group representations. EST explicitly mixes information across sampled orientations, unlike prior orientation-wise spherical operations, while retaining a strong approximate equivariant inductive bias through near-uniform spherical sampling. As demonstrated by our experiments on challenging benchmarks like OC20, MPtrj and QM9, EST-based models achieve state-of-the-art performance. For the complex molecular systems within OC20, small models empowered by EST can outperform some larger models and those using additional data. We characterize the ideal closed-domain condition under which the continuous operation is exactly equivariant and empirically quantify the finite-sampling accuracy--equivariance--memory trade-off used in practice.

item.title: From Images to Signals: Are Large Vision Models Useful for Time Series Analysis?
item.description: arXiv:2505.24030v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Transformer-based models have gained increasing attention in time series research, driving interest in Large Language Models (LLMs) and foundation models for time series analysis. As the field moves toward multi-modality, Large Vision Models (LVMs) are emerging as a promising direction. In the past, the effectiveness of Transformer and LLMs in time series has been debated. When it comes to LVMs, a similar question arises: are LVMs truely useful for time series analysis? To address it, we design and conduct the first principled study involving 4 LVMs, 8 imaging methods, 18 datasets and 26 baselines across both high-level (classification) and low-level (forecasting) tasks, with extensive ablation analysis. Our findings indicate LVMs are indeed useful for time series classification but face challenges in forecasting. Although effective, the contemporary best LVM forecasters are limited to specific types of LVMs and imaging methods, exhibit a bias toward forecasting periods, and have limited ability to utilize long look-back windows. We hope our findings could serve as a cornerstone for future research on LVM- and multimodal-based solutions to different time series tasks.

item.title: BNPO: Beta Normalization Policy Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2506.02864v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Reinforcement learning with rule-based, binary-valued reward functions has been shown to significantly enhance the reasoning capabilities of large language models. These models typically rely on REINFORCE-based policy optimization methods, such as REINFORCE with baseline and group relative policy optimization (GRPO). However, a key limitation is that existing methods either ignore reward normalization or use static normalization schemes, which fail to adapt to the evolving policy during training. This mismatch can lead to unstable gradient estimates and hinder training stability. To address this issue, we propose Beta Normalization Policy Optimization (BNPO), a novel method that adaptively normalizes rewards using a Beta distribution with dynamically updated parameters. By aligning normalization with the changing policy distribution, BNPO enables more accurate, lower-variance gradient estimation and promotes stable training dynamics. We provide theoretical analysis showing that BNPO reduces variance and generalizes both REINFORCE and GRPO under binary-valued rewards. In addition, we introduce an advantage decomposition mechanism to extend BNPO to more complex reward settings. Experimental results demonstrate that BNPO achieves state-of-the-art performance among policy optimization methods on reasoning tasks.

item.title: AblationBench: Evaluating Automated Planning of Ablations in Empirical AI Research
item.description: arXiv:2507.08038v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Language model agents are increasingly used to automate scientific research, yet evaluating their scientific contributions remains a challenge. A key mechanism to obtain such insights is through ablation experiments. To this end, we introduce AblationBench, a benchmark suite for evaluating agents on ablation planning tasks in empirical AI research. It includes two tasks: AuthorAblation, which helps authors propose ablation experiments based on a method section and contains 83 instances, and ReviewerAblation, which helps reviewers find missing ablations in a full paper and contains 350 instances. For both tasks, we develop LM-based judges that serve as an automatic evaluation framework. Our experiments with frontier LMs show that these tasks remain challenging, with the best-performing LM system identifying only 45% of the original ablations on average, below human-level performance. We observe an inverse performance trend between the author and reviewer tasks, which we attribute to differences in model grounding. Lastly, we analyze the limitations of current LMs on these tasks, and find that chain-of-thought prompting outperforms an agent-based approach. Our data is available on https://huggingface.co/collections/ai-coscientist/ablationbench, and our code is available on https://github.com/ai-scientist-bench/ablation-bench .

item.title: End-to-End On-Device Quantization-Aware Training for LLMs at Inference Cost
item.description: arXiv:2509.00031v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Quantization reduces the deployment cost of large language models (LLMs). However, post-training quantization (PTQ) cannot fine-tune model parameters and often degrades accuracy in low-bit settings, while quantization-aware training (QAT) requires backpropagation and incurs high memory overhead. We propose ZeroQAT, a zeroth-order QAT framework supporting both weight and activation quantization. By using forward-only gradient estimation, ZeroQAT removes backpropagation and substantially reduces memory and computation while retaining end-to-end optimization benefits. We further introduce a lightweight variant of ZeroQAT for quantized fine-tuning, which freezes and pre-quantizes most parameters to further cut memory usage. Experiments show that ZeroQAT consistently outperforms representative PTQ and QAT baselines while requiring significantly less memory. For example, ZeroQAT enables fine-tuning of a 13B model at extremely low bit-widths (e.g., 2-4 bits) on a single 8GB GPU, and even allows fine-tuning a 6.7B model on a OnePlus 12 smartphone, demonstrating its practicality for end-to-end QAT on resource-limited edge devices.

item.title: Align Your Query: Representation Alignment for Multimodality Medical Object Detection
item.description: arXiv:2510.02789v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Medical object detection suffers when a single detector is trained on mixed medical modalities (e.g., CXR, CT, MRI) due to heterogeneous statistics and disjoint representation spaces. To address this challenge, we turn to representation alignment, an approach that has proven effective for bringing features from different sources into a shared space. Specifically, we target the representations of DETR-style object queries and propose a simple, detector-agnostic framework to align them with modality context. First, we define modality tokens: compact, text-derived embeddings encoding imaging modality that are lightweight and require no extra annotations. We integrate the modality tokens into the detection process via Multimodality Context Attention (MoCA), mixing object-query representations via self-attention to propagate modality context within the query set. This preserves DETR-style architectures and adds negligible latency while injecting modality cues into object queries. We further introduce QueryREPA, a short pretraining stage that aligns query representations to their modality tokens using a task-specific contrastive objective with modality-balanced batches. Together, MoCA and QueryREPA produce modality-aware, class-faithful queries that transfer effectively to downstream training. Across diverse modalities trained altogether, the proposed approach consistently improves AP with minimal overhead and no architectural modifications, offering a practical path toward robust multimodality medical object detection.

item.title: Enhancing Neural Code Representation with Additional Context
item.description: arXiv:2510.12082v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Automated program comprehension underpins many software engineering tasks, from code summarisation to clone detection. While recent deep learning models have achieved strong results, they typically rely on source code alone, overlooking contextual signals such as version history or structural relationships. We conduct an empirical study of how enriching code representations with such signals affects model performance on four tasks: code clone detection, code classification, code summarisation, and vulnerability detection, using three datasets (SeSaMe, CodeSearchNet-Java, Vul4J). We evaluate five foundational code models (CodeBERT, GraphCodeBERT, CodeT5, PLBART, ASTNN) and seven code-specialised LLMs (CodeLlama, Qwen2.5-Coder, DeepSeek-Coder), comparing prompt-based context injection against fine-tuned use of context. Context improves classification for all five foundational models and, after fine-tuning, for most LLMs. For summarisation, the effect depends on the model family: version history improves all four foundational models on every metric, whereas prompt-level context helps two of the seven LLMs and hurts the other five. Combining context types reaches up to +21.48% macro-F1 in code classification and +15.04% F1 in clone detection. A human evaluation of CodeT5 summaries on 100 Java snippets ranks context-augmented summaries significantly higher for Accuracy and Content Adequacy. An exploratory vulnerability detection evaluation provides initial evidence of transfer to security-oriented tasks.

item.title: ReefNet: A Large-Scale Dataset and Benchmark for Fine-Grained Coral Reef Recognition
item.description: arXiv:2510.16822v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Coral reef monitoring requires scalable recognition of visually similar taxa across heterogeneous underwater surveys. We introduce ReefNet, a public dataset that aligns approximately 925K hard-coral point annotations from 76 CoralNet sources and an independently collected Al-Wajh dataset with the World Register of Marine Species taxonomy. A stratified expert audit of 8,962 patches guides filtering to a 479,027-annotation benchmark with 39 labels: 38 genera and the family Fungiidae. Expert agreement is 92% on the retained audit subset, rather than an exhaustive accuracy estimate. We evaluate pretrained models through zero-shot recognition, few-shot adaptation, and full fine-tuning, each on within-source ReefNet and held-out-source Al-Wajh tests. Biological vision-language pretraining provides the strongest zero-shot results; supervised adaptation substantially improves recognition, with DINOv2 reaching 65.79% macro recall on Al-Wajh. Matched text-description experiments improve all four evaluated MLLMs on Al-Wajh, while a GPT-5.4 reasoning ablation does not improve over direct classification. Long-tail recognition, label uncertainty, and geographic imbalance remain challenges. ReefNet provides a taxonomically grounded resource for studying these challenges; the Al-Wajh test is a regional stress test rather than evidence of global robustness. Public data and resource links are documented in the supplement.

item.title: AURA: A Reinforcement Learning Framework for AI-Driven Adaptive Conversational Surveys
item.description: arXiv:2510.27126v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Conventional online surveys provide limited personalization, often resulting in low engagement and superficial responses. Although AI survey chatbots improve convenience, most are still reactive: they rely on fixed dialogue trees or static prompt templates and therefore cannot adapt within a session to fit individual users, which leads to generic follow-ups and weak response quality. We address these limitations with AURA (Adaptive Understanding through Reinforcement Learning for Assessment), a reinforcement learning framework for AI-driven adaptive conversational surveys. AURA quantifies response quality using a four-dimensional LSDE metric (Length, Self-disclosure, Emotion, and Specificity) and selects follow-up question types via an epsilon-greedy policy that updates the expected quality gain within each session. Initialized with priors extracted from 96 prior campus-climate conversations (467 total chatbot-user exchanges), the system balances exploration and exploitation across 10-15 dialogue exchanges, dynamically adapting to individual participants in real time. In controlled evaluations, AURA achieved a +0.076 mean gain in response quality and a statistically significant improvement over non-adaptive baselines (p=0.044, d=0.66), driven by a 63% reduction in specification prompts and a 10x increase in validation behavior. These results demonstrate that reinforcement learning can give survey chatbots improved adaptivity, transforming static questionnaires into interactive, self-improving assessment systems.

item.title: Physics Steering: Causal Control of Cross-Domain Concepts in a Physics Foundation Model
item.description: arXiv:2511.20798v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Foundation models trained on text and images have been shown to develop abstract internal features that align with human concepts and that can be directly manipulated via activation steering to alter model behaviour. Whether scientific foundation models learn similarly abstract and domain-general representations has remained an open question. Inspired by recent work identifying single directions in activation space that control complex behaviours in large language models, we show that Walrus, a large physics foundation model, learns linearly steerable representations of physical phenomena. By computing the difference between activations representing contrasting physical regimes, we identify single directions in activation space that correspond to vorticity, diffusion, and even temporal progression. We find that injecting these concept directions back into the model during inference enables fine-grained causal control: vortices can be induced or removed, diffusion enhanced or suppressed, and simulations sped up or slowed down. Moreover, directions derived from one physical system also steer the behaviour of other physical systems, suggesting that they are domain-general. These results provide early evidence that scientific foundation models can learn general representations of physical principles, and further support for the Linear Representation Hypothesis.

item.title: Predicting Public Health Impacts of Electricity Usage
item.description: arXiv:2511.22031v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The electric power sector is a leading source of air pollutant emissions, impacting the public health of nearly every community. Although regulatory measures have reduced air pollutants, fossil fuels remain a significant component of the energy supply, highlighting the need for more advanced demand-side approaches to reduce the public health impacts. To enable health-informed demand-side management, we introduce HealthPredictor, a domain-specific AI model that provides an end-to-end pipeline linking electricity use to public health outcomes. The model comprises three components: a fuel mix predictor that estimates the contribution of different generation sources, an air quality converter that models pollutant emissions and atmospheric dispersion, and a health impact assessor that translates resulting pollutant changes into monetized health damages. Across multiple regions in the United States, our health-driven optimization framework yields substantially lower prediction errors in terms of public health impacts than fuel mix-driven baselines. A case study on electric vehicle charging schedules illustrates the public health gains enabled by our method and the actionable guidance it can offer for health-informed energy management. Overall, this work shows how AI models can be explicitly designed to enable health-informed energy management for advancing public health and broader societal well-being. Our datasets and code are released at: https://github.com/Ren-Research/Health-Impact-Predictor.

item.title: Limitations of Using Identical Distributions for Training and Testing When Learning Boolean Functions
item.description: arXiv:2512.00791v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: When the distributions of the training and test data do not coincide, the problem of understanding generalization becomes considerably more complex, prompting a variety of questions. Prior work has shown that, for some fixed learning methods, there are scenarios where training on a distribution different from the test distribution improves generalization. However, these results do not account for the possibility of choosing, for each training distribution, the optimal learning algorithm, leaving open whether the observed benefits stem from the mismatch itself or from suboptimality of the learner. In this work, we address this question. That is, we study whether it is always optimal for the training distribution to be identical to the test distribution when the learner is allowed to be optimally adapted to the training distribution. Surprisingly, when we restrict our attention to efficient learners, i.e., those running in polynomial time, and assume the existence of one-way functions, the answer is negative. In other words, matching the training and test distributions is not always optimal.

item.title: Evolutionary Architecture Search through Grammar-Based Sequence Alignment
item.description: arXiv:2512.04992v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Neural architecture search (NAS) in expressive search spaces is a computationally hard problem, but it also holds the potential to automatically discover completely novel and performant architectures. To achieve this we need effective search algorithms that can identify powerful components and reuse them in new candidate architectures. In this paper, we introduce two adapted variants of the Smith-Waterman algorithm for local sequence alignment and use them to compute the edit distance in a grammar-based evolutionary architecture search. These algorithms enable us to efficiently calculate a distance metric for neural architectures and to generate a set of hybrid offspring from two parent models. This facilitates the deployment of crossover-based search heuristics, allows us to perform a thorough analysis on the architectural loss landscape, and track population diversity during search. We highlight how our method vastly improves computational complexity over previous work and enables us to efficiently compute shortest paths between architectures. When instantiating the crossover in evolutionary searches, we achieve competitive results, outperforming competing methods. Future work can build upon this new tool, discovering novel components that can be used more broadly across neural architecture design, and broadening its applications beyond NAS.

item.title: MCGI: Manifold-Consistent Graph Indexing for Billion-Scale Disk-Resident Vector Search
item.description: arXiv:2601.01930v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Graph-based Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) search often suffers from performance degradation in high-dimensional spaces due to the Euclidean-Geodesic mismatch, where greedy routing diverges from the underlying data manifold. To address this challenge, this paper presents Manifold-Consistent Graph Indexing (MCGI), a geometry-aware and disk-resident indexing method that leverages Local Intrinsic Dimensionality (LID) to allocate the search effort of a graph index according to the intrinsic geometry of data. Specifically, MCGI estimates the LID around each query from the distances that its own search has already computed and resizes the candidate list of the query once, so that queries in high-LID regions receive longer lists while queries in low-LID regions terminate earlier; the estimate itself costs no additional disk reads. Theoretical analysis shows that the success probability of any fixed search list decays exponentially with the LID of the query. At matched high recall, MCGI raises the query throughput of DiskANN on the same standard Vamana index by up to $1.43\times$ on three million-scale benchmarks and by up to $1.24\times$ on the billion-scale SIFT1B and Deep1B.

item.title: Remote Sensing Change Detection via Weak Temporal Supervision
item.description: arXiv:2601.02126v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Semantic change detection in remote sensing aims to identify land cover changes between bi-temporal image pairs. Progress in this area has been limited by the scarcity of annotated datasets, as pixel-level annotation is costly and time-consuming. To address this, recent methods leverage synthetic data or generate artificial change pairs, but transferring change detection models across datasets and acquisition conditions remains challenging. In this work, we introduce a weak temporal supervision strategy that leverages additional temporal observations of existing single-temporal datasets, without requiring any new annotations. Specifically, we extend single-date remote sensing datasets with new observations acquired at different times and train a change detection model by assuming that real bi-temporal pairs mostly contain no change, while pairing images from different locations to generate change examples. To handle the inherent noise in these weak labels, we employ an object-aware change map generation and an iterative refinement process. We validate our approach on extended versions of the FLAIR and IAILD aerial datasets, showing competitive zero-shot and low-data regime performance. Lastly, we showcase results over large areas in France, highlighting the scalability potential of our method.

item.title: Outcome-Based RL Provably Leads Transformers to Reason, but Only With the Right Data
item.description: arXiv:2601.15158v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Transformers trained via Reinforcement Learning (RL) with outcome-based supervision can spontaneously develop the ability to generate intermediate reasoning steps (Chain-of-Thought). Yet the mechanism by which sparse rewards drive policy gradient to discover such systematic reasoning remains poorly understood. We address this by analyzing the policy gradient dynamics of single-layer linear Transformers on a synthetic graph traversal task that cannot be solved without Chain-of-Thought but admits a simple iterative solution. We prove that despite training solely on final-answer correctness, policy gradient drives the Transformer to converge to a structured, interpretable algorithm that iteratively traverses the graph vertex-by-vertex. We characterize the distributional properties required for this emergence, identifying the critical role of "simple examples": instances requiring fewer reasoning steps. When the training distribution places sufficient mass on these simpler examples, the Transformer learns a generalizable traversal strategy that extrapolates to longer chains; when this mass vanishes, policy gradient learning becomes infeasible. We corroborate our theoretical results through experiments on synthetic data and with real-world language models on mathematical reasoning tasks, validating that our theoretical findings carry over to practical settings.

item.title: Fast Statistical Rates for Flow Matching without Curvature Assumptions
item.description: arXiv:2601.20250v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Flow-based generative models have emerged as an efficient alternative to diffusion models. We study the sample complexity of learning a target distribution in Wasserstein distance via flow matching, which learns a velocity field transporting a base distribution to the target. Under exact empirical risk minimization over a fixed network class and standard assumptions on the architecture and data distribution, we show that any squared-loss flow-matching variant including rectified flow with bounded derivatives achieves $\widetilde{O}(\varepsilon^{-2})$ sample complexity for the statistical term with the Wasserstein guarantee taking the form $W_2 \le K(\varepsilon + C\varepsilon_{app})$, where $\varepsilon_{app}$ is the approximation error of the network class. This improves upon existing $\widetilde{O}(\varepsilon^{-4})$ guarantees and does not require the Polyak--Lojasiewicz condition in the statistical analysis. Instead, we exploit a structural property of the squared-loss objective - it induces an approximate Bernstein condition that directly ties the variance of the excess loss to the excess risk up to additive approximation-error. This condition enables a localized Rademacher complexity analysis yielding fast $O(1/n)$ rates. The flow-matching schedule enters the leading statistical prefactor through the Lipschitz constant of the pointwise loss, which we characterize explicitly for standard schedules.

item.title: MemSkill: Learning and Evolving Memory Skills for Self-Evolving Agents
item.description: arXiv:2602.02474v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Most Large Language Model (LLM) agent memory systems rely on a small set of static, hand-designed operations for extracting memory. These fixed procedures hard-code human priors about what to store and how to revise memory, making them rigid under diverse interaction patterns and inefficient on long histories. To this end, we present \textbf{MemSkill}, which reframes these operations as learnable and evolvable memory skills, structured and reusable routines for extracting, consolidating, and pruning information from interaction traces. Inspired by the design philosophy of agent skills, MemSkill employs a \emph{controller} that learns to select a small set of relevant skills, paired with an LLM-based \emph{executor} that produces skill-guided memories. Beyond learning skill selection, MemSkill introduces a \emph{designer} that periodically reviews hard cases where selected skills yield incorrect or incomplete memories, and evolves the skill set by proposing refinements and new skills. Together, MemSkill forms a closed-loop procedure that improves both the skill-selection policy and the skill set itself. Experiments on LoCoMo, LongMemEval, HotpotQA, and ALFWorld demonstrate that MemSkill improves task performance over strong baselines and generalizes well across settings. Further analyses shed light on how skills evolve, offering insights toward more adaptive, self-evolving memory management for LLM agents. Code is available at https://github.com/ViktorAxelsen/MemSkill

item.title: Temporal Pair Consistency for Flow Matching
item.description: arXiv:2602.04908v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Flow-matching-style generative models learn time-dependent vector fields, but standard objectives supervise each timestep independently, leaving shared-path temporal structure unused. We introduce Temporal Pair Consistency (TPC), a simple training-time objective that couples velocity predictions at paired timesteps along the same probability path. TPC leaves the architecture, probability path, sampler, and inference-time computation unchanged. Under matched backbones, training budgets, solvers, and numbers of function evaluations, TPC improves sample quality across flow matching, OT-CFM, rectified flow, DiT-style backbones, and MeanFlow. On CIFAR-10, TPC improves FM from 6.35 to 3.19 FID and OT-CFM from 3.58 to 2.90 FID at the same NFE. Mechanism diagnostics show lower measured gradient variance, higher paired-gradient correlation, and reduced temporal roughness, while random and local pairing controls are substantially weaker. Higher-resolution ImageNet experiments further show consistent gains for DiT-XL/2 at 256 and 512 resolution and for MeanFlow at 256 resolution, all at matched inference cost.

item.title: EpiFlow: Bridging Safety and Performance in Offline Reinforcement Learning via Epigraph-Guided Flow Matching
item.description: arXiv:2602.08054v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Offline reinforcement learning (RL) offers a promising framework for deploying autonomous systems in safety-critical settings without the risks of online exploration. However, learning policies that simultaneously achieve high performance and strong safety guarantees from fixed datasets remains a fundamental challenge. Many existing safe offline RL approaches typically rely on soft constraint formulations, which may permit safety violations and are sensitive to distributional shift. In contrast, formal methods such as Hamilton--Jacobi (HJ) reachability and Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) provide rigorous safety guarantees, but often yield overly conservative solutions, often neglecting performance. In this work, we bridge this gap by formulating safe offline RL as a state-constrained optimal control problem, where safety is enforced through hard state constraints and performance is captured via a reward function. The resulting value function satisfies a Hamilton--Jacobi--Bellman (HJB) equation, which we approximate using offline RL on fixed datasets by learning an epigraph feasibility value function and extracting policies via flow matching. This formulation enables principled integration of safety guarantees with data-driven policy optimization. Empirically, across safety-critical benchmarks including boat navigation, Safety-Gymnasium, and Bullet-Safety-Gym tasks, our approach achieves competitive returns while exhibiting near-zero constraint violations, demonstrating a favorable balance between safety and performance in the offline setting.

item.title: Fast and General Automatic Differentiation for Finite-State Methods
item.description: arXiv:2602.12300v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We propose a new method, that we coined the ``morphism-trick'', to integrate custom implementations of vector-Jacobian products in automatic differentiation softwares, applicable to a wide range of semiring-based computations. Our approach leads to efficient and semiring-agnostic implementations of the backward pass of dynamic programming algorithms. For the particular case of finite-state methods, we introduce an algorithm that computes and differentiates the $\oplus$-sum of all paths' weight of a finite-state automaton. Results show that, with minimal effort from the user, our novel library allows computing the gradient of a function w.r.t. to the weights of a finite state automaton orders of magnitude faster than state-of-the-art automatic differentiation systems. Implementations are made available via an open-source library distributed under a permissive license.

item.title: Human-AI Collaboration in Large Language Model-Integrated Building Energy Management Systems: The Role of User Domain Knowledge and AI Literacy
item.description: arXiv:2602.16140v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This study aimed to comprehend how user domain knowledge and artificial intelligence (AI) literacy impact the effective use of human-AI interactive building energy management system (BEMS). While prior studies have investigated the potential of integrating large language models (LLMs) into BEMS or building energy modeling, very few studies have examined how user interact with such systems. We conducted a systematic role-playing experiment, where 85 human subjects interacted with an advanced generative pre-trained transformer (OpenAI GPT-4o). Participants were tasked with identifying the top five behavioral changes that could reduce home energy use with the GPT model that functioned as an LLM-integrated BEMS. Then, the collected prompt-response data and participant conclusions were analyzed using an analytical framework that hierarchically assessed and scored human-AI interactions and their home energy analysis approaches. Also, participants were classified into four groups based on their self-evaluated domain knowledge of building energy use and AI literacy, and Kruskal-Wallis H tests with post-hoc pairwise comparisons were conducted across 20 quantifiable metrics. Key takeaways include: most participants employed concise prompts (median: 16.2 words) and relied heavily on GPT's analytical capabilities; and notably, only 1 of 20 metrics, appliance identification rate, showed statistically significant group differences (p=0.037), driven by AI literacy rather than domain knowledge, suggesting an equalizing effect of LLMs across expertise levels. This study provides foundational insights into human-AI collaboration dynamics and promising development directions in the context of LLM-integrated BEMS and contributes to realizing human-centric LLM-integrated energy systems.

item.title: Interpretability-by-Design with Accurate Locally Additive Models and Conditional Feature Effects
item.description: arXiv:2602.16503v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Generalized additive models (GAMs) offer high interpretability through independent univariate feature effects but underfit when interactions are present in data. GA$^2$Ms add selected pairwise interactions, which improves accuracy, but sacrifices interpretability. We propose Conditionally Additive Local Models (CALMs), a new model class that narrows this trade-off: it stays close to GAMs in interpretability and close to GA$^2$Ms in accuracy. CALMs allow multiple univariate shape functions per feature, each active in different regions of the input space. These regions are defined independently for each feature as simple logical conditions (thresholds) on the features it interacts with. As a result, effects remain locally additive while varying across subregions to capture interactions. We further propose a principled distillation-based training pipeline that identifies homogeneous regions with limited interactions and fits interpretable shape functions via region-aware backfitting. Experiments on diverse classification and regression tasks show that CALMs never underperform GAMs, often beat them and achieve accuracy broadly comparable to GA$^2$Ms, while preserving the univariate auditability that GA$^2$Ms forfeit.

item.title: Same Words, Different Judgments: How Preferences Vary Across Modalities
item.description: arXiv:2602.22710v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Preference-based reinforcement learning (PbRL) is the dominant framework for aligning AI systems to human preferences. However, evaluation protocols for such data were designed for text and have not been validated for speech. We present the first intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC)-based, controlled cross-modal study of human and synthetic preference annotations, comparing text and audio evaluations of identical semantic content across 100 prompts. We show that achieving \textit{good} (audio) to \textit{near good} (text) agreement within either modality (ICC(2,$k$) $\approx$ .81 audio, .74 text) requires $\sim$9 raters and modalities show marked differences in how people report preferences: audio raters exhibit narrower decision thresholds, reduced length bias, and more user-oriented evaluation criteria, with near-chance cross-modality agreement. We demonstrate that synthetic ratings can be used to effectively predict inter-rater agreement, thus serving as an early signal for stimulus selection and proxy for human annotations. Together, these findings argue that evaluation protocols for audio preference data require modality-specific design rather than direct adaptation from text. Code, data, and the audio corpus are available at: https://huggingface.co/datasets/sciminds/same-words-different-judgements

item.title: Preconditioned Flow Matching
item.description: arXiv:2603.02337v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Flow matching (FM) learns vector fields by regressing stochastic velocity targets along intermediate distributions $p_t$. We identify a geometric optimization bottleneck in this regression problem: when the covariance $\Sigma_t$ of $p_t$ is ill-conditioned, gradient-based training rapidly fits high-variance directions while making slow progress along low-variance ones. In an exactly solvable Gaussian setting, we prove that the excess risk is weighted by $\Sigma_t$, and that both gradient descent and stochastic gradient descent inherit condition-number-dependent convergence. We then extend the analysis to Gaussian mixtures, showing that multimodality does not average away this effect; instead, the slowest and worst-conditioned component can control optimization. Motivated by this analysis, we propose $\textit{preconditioned flow matching}$, a precondition-then-match framework that transforms the target distribution into a more isotropic representation, trains the main flow in the transformed space, and maps generated samples back through the inverse transformation. We show theoretically that preconditioning reshapes the intermediate FM path and improves its conditioning. Across controlled Gaussian and Gaussian-mixture experiments, latent MNIST and other high resolution image datasets up to $512{\times}512$ resolution, preconditioning improves path-conditioning diagnostics, low-eigenvalue recovery, FID, MMD, precision, and recall. Compute-matched baselines and preconditioner-quality ablations further show that the gains are not explained merely by additional preconditioner parameters, but by improved geometry of the downstream flow matching problem. GitHub: https://github.com/ahxmeds/preconditioned-flow-matching.git.

item.title: Knowledge Localization in Mixture-of-Experts LLMs Using Cross-Lingual Inconsistency
item.description: arXiv:2603.17102v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Modern LLMs continue to exhibit significant variance in behavior across languages, such as being able to recall factual information in some languages but not others. While typically studied as a problem to be mitigated, in this work, we propose leveraging this cross-lingual inconsistency as a tool for interpretability in mixture-of-experts (MoE) LLMs. Our knowledge localization framework contrasts routing for sets of languages where the model correctly recalls information from languages where it fails. This allows us to isolate model components that play a functional role in answering about a piece of knowledge. Our method proceeds in two stages: (1) querying the model with difficult factual questions across a diverse set of languages to generate "success" and "failure" activation buckets and then (2) applying a statistical contrastive analysis to the MoE router logits to identify experts important for knowledge. To validate the necessity of this small number of experts for answering a knowledge question, we deactivate them and re-ask the question. We find that despite only deactivating about 20 out of 6000 experts, the model no longer answers correctly in over 40% of cases. Generally, this method provides a realistic and scalable knowledge localization approach to address increasingly complex LLMs.

item.title: Spectral Alignment in Forward-Backward Representations via Temporal Abstraction
item.description: arXiv:2603.20103v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Forward-backward (FB) representations provide a powerful framework for learning the successor representation (SR) in continuous spaces by enforcing a low-rank factorization. However, a fundamental spectral mismatch often exists between the high-rank transition dynamics of continuous environments and the low-rank bottleneck of the FB architecture, making accurate low-rank representation learning difficult. In this work, we analyze temporal abstraction as a mechanism to mitigate this mismatch. By characterizing the spectral properties of the transition operator, we show that temporal abstraction acts analogously to a low-pass filter that suppresses high-frequency spectral components. This suppression reduces the effective rank of the induced SR while preserving a formal bound on the resulting value function error. Empirically, we show that this alignment is a key factor for stable FB learning, particularly at high discount factors where bootstrapping becomes error-prone.
